frameworks.name: Founder Dependency vs. Scalable Ownership
frameworks.definition: Two business models with identical $10M revenue and $2M profit yield drastically different wealth outcomes: founder-dependent (high hours, slow wealth accumulation) vs. scalable (founder-free, business valued at multiple of profit).

frameworks.name: Delegation Sequence: Inventory, Process, People
frameworks.definition: Transform founder dependency through: (1) self-inventory and time study documenting all tasks, (2) classify each task as green/yellow/red (delegable/installable/unfillable), (3) install green tasks first, yellow second, red last.

claims.text: Two identical $10M-revenue businesses with $2M profit produce dramatically different wealth outcomes depending on whether the owner is required to work 80+ hours weekly (narrow wealth accumulation via salary and savings) versus owns the business like a stock (exponential wealth via business valuation multiple). At identical $10M/$2M financials, the founder-free owner is richer by 10-20x despite same annual profit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Owner fully extracted from day-to-day operations
claims.mechanism: The scalable business trades at a 6x profit multiple while founder-dependent profit is divided by 2 (taxes) then by spending needs, yielding 20-30x valuation gap.

numbers.axis: Business ownership model impact on net worth

anchors.region: Founder-dependent, 80 hrs/week, $2M profit after tax = $1M, minus $500k living = $500k/year savings
Founder-free, business valued at 6x profit ($12M), + $500k new profit × 6 multiple
anchors.value: $3M added to net worth on same $500k profit increase

bounded_by: Does not apply to founder-dependent consulting or solo service practices below $2M revenue
Assumes business can be valued at 6x profit (requires systems, not founder dependency)

claims.text: The wealth accumulation model is exponentially more efficient through business multiples than through salary and savings. A 20x difference in wealth outcomes emerges from replacing founder labor with systems: one path yields linear $500k/year savings (after tax + living costs); the other yields $3M net worth jump from profit multiple leverage on the same additional $500k profit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder removes themselves from day-to-day operations
claims.mechanism: Profit multiplied by business valuation multiple (6x for scalable service businesses) compounds wealth orders of magnitude faster than after-tax salary divided by annual needs.
bounded_by: Does not apply to pure personal-service models (surgery, law) where founder replaces client value
Requires documented processes enabling founder exit

claims.text: The first step to founder extraction is a self-inventory: list everything you do, break each into granular component tasks, then classify each task by whether it is delegable (green), requires a one-time process installation (yellow), or requires hiring a person you do not yet have (red). Complete green tasks before yellow, yellow before red.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: A time study (recording one-word activity tags every 15 minutes in a spreadsheet) over one week reveals the actual task portfolio and becomes the most productive week of the founder's life by forcing task-level visibility. Solo founders should run time studies before delegating; managers should run them on key personnel to diagnose key-man risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has not documented their own activities
claims.mechanism: Explicit task visibility forces improvement by establishing a feedback loop: founders become aware of task density and can begin to delegate or streamline.

claims.text: For each task, classify by color: green = can delegate immediately to existing team; yellow = requires a one-time project or process installation by the founder but then becomes delegable; red = founder lacks the required skill or does not have the person for it yet. Solve greens first (quick wins, fast delegation), yellows second (time-intensive but one-time), reds last (long-term hiring or skill-building).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Inventory has been completed and tasks are categorized
claims.mechanism: Prioritizing easy delegations (green) first creates momentum and quick wins, freeing founder time before tackling complex process builds (yellow) and hiring (red).

claims.text: For each task on the inventory, decision rules (if-then statements) must be documented so team members can handle common scenarios without founder input. Example: customer requests address change, billing cadence change, flavor change, billing cycle change, refund/cancellation — each needs a clear decision tree so support staff operate independently.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Support or operations role has multiple repetitive decision points
Role serves customers or internal stakeholders
claims.mechanism: Explicit decision trees remove founder approval bottleneck, enabling faster team iteration and customer resolution.

claims.text: Approval authorities must be set by spending threshold: decisions under $500 require no approval; decisions $500-$1,000 can be approved by ops staff without founder; decisions above threshold require founder sign-off. Cap total spending per role (e.g., $5,000/month per person) so discretionary spending is bounded.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Team has >5 people making operational decisions
claims.mechanism: Tiered spending authority distributes decision-making, freeing founder from low-leverage approvals while maintaining financial controls via monthly audits and per-person caps.

anchors.value: Approved by ops staff, not founder

bounded_by: Does not apply to revenue-generating decisions (sales pricing, customer acceptance)
Does not scale to very large organizations where subsidiary approval layers are needed

claims.text: Founder over-delivery (working 80 hours weekly while replacements work standard 40 hours) masks true business profitability. When founder removes themselves, business performance typically decays 25-35% initially as replacement efficiency lags. Systems must be designed to absorb this handoff efficiency loss.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has been personal delivery vehicle
Business being prepared for founder exit or delegation
claims.mechanism: Founder efficiency advantage erodes when founder removes themselves; replacement operator requires documented systems, training time, and has lower context familiarity, reducing output 25-35% until ramp.
bounded_by: Decay percentage varies by role complexity: high-skill roles show more decay, administrative tasks show less

examples.text: Alex ran Prestige Labs, a supplement company. When the support manager said it was hard to onboard new team members, he asked her to list all customer requests. She rattled off: change my address, change my card, change my flavor, change my billing cadence, cancel/refund. These five scenarios became the decision tree. Each request now had a single clear path, and new support staff could resolve customer issues without founder involvement.

Alex tracked surprise dinners for visiting clients at the company headquarters. His team would see two or three clients who seemed to mesh well and would spontaneously book a five-star restaurant as a surprise-and-delight gesture. After a month, the bill was $250,000 in surprise dinners. When he reviewed the data, he found that removing the dinners did not change customer satisfaction scores, reviews, or happiness metrics. The discretionary spending authority experiment showed that feel-good gestures could be over-indexed against actual value created.

practices.text: Run a time study once per year: record your activity in 15-minute blocks for one full week. Note one word per block describing what you did. This single week becomes your most productive week because it forces visibility into task allocation.

Document all recurring decisions as if-then rules. When a customer contacts you with a request, if it is a duplicate request type, you should have a clear protocol that team members can execute without escalation.

Set approval thresholds by dollar amount and role. Below $500: no approval required. $500-$1,000: ops staff approves. Above $1,000: founder approves. Use monthly caps to constrain total discretionary authority per person.

Prioritize task delegation in three phases: green tasks first (quick delegation to existing staff), yellow tasks second (one-time process builds), red tasks last (new hires or skill development). This sequence maximizes early wins.
